chapters.name: Chapter 1: Building the core of your CV

lessons.title: Lesson 1: CV or resume: what changes from country to country
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the right CV length, format and personal details for the country you are applying to.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job in a named country, you will choose the CV format, length and personal details that the country and employer expect, following the job ad's instructions and leaving out ID and passport numbers.
A CV (curriculum vitae) is a short document that shows an employer your skills, work and education. In the United States and Canada it is usually called a resume and is often one or two pages. Most countries use the word CV. For most jobs, two pages is a safe maximum; long academic CVs are only for research and university posts.
Personal details change by country. Employers in the US, Canada and the UK usually do not want a photo, your age, marital status or religion, because of rules against discrimination. In many countries in Africa, the Middle East, Asia and Latin America (for example Nigeria, Egypt, Morocco, India, the Philippines, Mexico and Colombia) many employers still expect a photo, date of birth or nationality. In Senegal or Côte d'Ivoire, the CV is usually written in French.
There is no single world rule, so follow three sources in this order: the job ad's own instructions, the employer's careers page, and then the usual practice in that country. If the ad asks for a photo, use a plain, professional head-and-shoulders photo. If you apply in Europe, many employers know the free Europass CV format.
Some things never go in a CV anywhere: your national ID, passport or social security number, bank details, or a copy of your passport. A real employer asks for those only after an offer, through a safe process.
Step by step:
- Read the job ad for instructions: language, format, photo, length, how to apply.
- Check the employer's careers page.
- Look up the usual CV practice for that country.
- Decide: length (1-2 pages), photo or no photo, which personal details.
- Leave out ID, passport and bank numbers every time.
Words to know:
- CV: curriculum vitae: a short document listing your skills, work and education for an employer.
- Resume: the usual US and Canadian name for a CV, often one or two pages.
- Europass: a free CV format and tool from the European Union, known by many employers in Europe.
- Discrimination: treating someone unfairly because of things like age, sex, religion or family status.
Official sources:
- Europass: Create your Europass CV (European Union)
Try it now: Pick two countries where you might work, for example your own country and one abroad. For each, write on paper: the language of the CV, the length, photo yes or no, and which personal details to include. Then find one real job ad in each and check whether it gives its own instructions.
You can now choose the CV length, language, photo and personal details for a country, and say what never goes in a CV.

check.q: A job ad from a company in Canada asks for a resume. What personal details do you leave out?
options: Your photo, age and marital status
check.why: Canadian and US employers usually do not want a photo, age or marital status.

check.q: Which item should never be in a CV, in any country?
check.why: ID and passport numbers can be used to steal your identity; employers ask for them only after an offer.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Your header and profile: the first ten seconds
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a CV header and a 3-4 line profile for one kind of job.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own information, you will write a CV header and a profile of 3 to 4 lines aimed at one kind of job, with working contact details and no spelling mistakes.
Recruiters often look at a CV for only a few seconds before deciding to read on. The top of the page must tell them who you are and what you can do.
The header has your full name, a phone number with the country code (for example +234 for Nigeria, +254 for Kenya, +63 for the Philippines), a professional email address, your city and country, and a LinkedIn link if you have one. A professional email is simple, like firstname.lastname@ plus your email provider, not a nickname.
The profile is 3 to 4 lines under the header. Say what you are (your job or field), your strongest skills or years of experience, one result, and what job you want. Example: "Customer service agent with 3 years in a busy mobile money shop in Accra. Served 80+ customers a day in English and Twi with very few complaints. Seeking a call center role."
Write one profile for one kind of job. If you apply for two different jobs, write two profiles.
Step by step:
- Write your full name in large text.
- Add phone with country code, professional email, city and country.
- Write line 1: what you are and your years of experience.
- Write lines 2-3: your best skills and one result.
- Write the last line: the job you want.
Words to know:
- Header: the top of the CV with your name and contact details.
- Profile: 3 to 4 lines under the header that sum up who you are and the job you want; also called a summary.
- Country code: the number added before a phone number when calling from another country, such as +233 for Ghana.
Try it now: Write your header. Check that your phone number has the country code and your email is professional. Then write a 3-4 line profile for one job you want. Read it aloud: can someone tell your job and your best result in ten seconds?
You can now write a CV header with working contact details and a short profile aimed at one job.

check.q: Which email address is best for a CV?
check.why: A simple name-based email looks professional.

check.q: You are applying from Kenya to an employer in another country. How should your phone number appear?
options: You should not give a phone number
check.why: The country code lets an employer abroad call you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing your work as results, including informal work
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write three experience entries that each start with an action verb and show a result.
This lesson builds toward: Given your work, study or community experience, paid or unpaid, you will write experience entries that start with an action verb and show a result, with at least one number or concrete detail in each entry.
Many CVs list duties: "Responsible for selling." Employers want to know what you achieved. Start each line with an action verb (served, sold, repaired, trained, organized, reduced) and add a result with a number or clear detail.
Duty: "Responsible for customers." Result: "Served about 60 customers a day and kept the shop's records in a notebook with no missing payments for 12 months."
Informal and unpaid work counts. Selling in a market in Lagos, repairing phones in Nairobi, helping run a family farm in Morocco, volunteering at church or a youth club, or doing online gig work are real experience. Give each one a clear title (for example "Self-employed trader" or "Volunteer youth coordinator"), the place, the dates and your results.
List your most recent work first. Use 2 to 4 lines per job. Never invent jobs, titles or numbers; if you estimate, say "about" and be ready to explain it in an interview.
Step by step:
- List every job, business, farm, volunteer or gig role you have had.
- Give each a clear title, place and dates (month and year).
- For each, write 2-4 lines that start with an action verb.
- Add a number or concrete detail to each line.
- Put the most recent first, and check every line is true.
Words to know:
- Action verb: a doing word that starts a CV line, like served, sold or repaired.
- Result: what changed because of your work, shown with a number or a clear detail.
- Informal work: work without a formal contract, such as market trading, family business or casual jobs.
Try it now: Choose three experiences, paid or unpaid. For each, write a title, place and dates, then two lines that start with an action verb and include a number or detail. Underline every number and check you could explain it to an interviewer.
You can now turn your paid and unpaid work into honest CV entries that show results.

options: Sold about 40 phone cases a week and trained 2 new staff
check.why: It starts with an action verb and gives numbers that show what you achieved.

check.q: You sold vegetables in a market for three years without a contract. What do you do?
options: List it as "Self-employed trader" with dates and results
Leave it out because it was informal
Call it a manager job at a large company
check.why: Informal work is real experience; give it a clear, honest title and results.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Making it fit the job, and staying safe

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Education, certificates and languages a foreign employer understands
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your qualifications and languages so an employer in another country can understand them.
This lesson builds toward: Given your certificates, training and languages, you will list your qualifications and language levels so an employer in another country can understand them, naming the school, the country, the year and a level a foreign reader can use.
An employer abroad may not know your school or your country's certificates, such as the WAEC or NECO certificate in West Africa, the KCSE in Kenya, the baccalauréat in Senegal or Morocco, or a TESDA National Certificate in the Philippines. For each one, write the full name, the school or awarding body, the city and country, the year, and a short plain explanation, for example "(national secondary school leaving certificate)".
For jobs or study in another country, the employer, a licensing board or an immigration office may ask for an official credential evaluation or recognition. In Europe, the ENIC-NARIC network points you to each country's recognition center; in the US and Canada, services such as World Education Services (WES) evaluate foreign qualifications. Ask the employer or the official office which one they accept before you pay for any evaluation.
Languages are a strong skill. Name each language and your level. Many employers understand the Common European Framework levels, A1 and A2 (basic), B1 and B2 (independent) and C1 and C2 (advanced), or simple words like "native", "fluent" or "basic". If you have a test result (for example IELTS, TOEFL or DELF), give the test and the year.
Short courses count too: online certificates, TVET programs, first aid or driving licenses. Put them under "Certificates and training" with the provider and year.
Step by step:
- List each qualification with full name, school or awarding body, city, country and year.
- Add a short plain explanation for local certificates.
- List each language with a level (native, fluent, B2, basic).
- Add test names and years if you have them.
- List short courses and licenses with the provider and year.
Words to know:
- Credential evaluation: an official report that explains what a foreign qualification equals in another country.
- ENIC-NARIC: a network of national centers that advise on recognizing qualifications from other countries.
- CEFR: Common European Framework of Reference: language levels from A1 (beginner) to C2 (very advanced).
- TVET: technical and vocational education and training: practical job training programs.
Official sources:
- ENIC-NARIC network: recognition of qualifications
- World Education Services (WES): credential evaluation for the US and Canada
- Europass: Common European Framework of Reference for language skills
Try it now: Write your Education, Certificates and Languages sections. Give every local certificate a short plain explanation, and give every language a level. Show it to someone from another country or region, or read it as if you were a foreign employer: is anything unclear?
You can now list your education, certificates and languages so an employer in another country understands them.

check.q: An employer in Germany may not know the KCSE. What do you write?
options: A higher degree you do not have
"KCSE (Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education), [school], Nairobi, Kenya, [year]"
check.why: The full name, school, place and year let a foreign employer understand it.

check.q: You speak Spanish at home and use English at work every day. How could you list them?
options: Spanish and English: perfect in every way
check.why: Name each language with a clear level an employer can use.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Tailoring your CV to one job ad
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Match your CV to a real job ad using its key words and a layout application systems can read.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real job ad, you will tailor your CV to the ad by using its key words and a layout that application systems can read, using at least five key words honestly and saving it as a clearly named PDF.
Sending the same CV to every job rarely works. Read the ad and underline the key words: job titles, skills, tools, languages and certificates (for example "customer service", "Excel", "bilingual French-English", "forklift license"). Where they are true for you, use the same words in your profile, skills and experience.
Many large employers and job sites use an applicant tracking system (ATS), software that reads CVs and searches them for key words. Help it read yours: use simple headings (Profile, Experience, Education, Skills, Languages), a common font, no text inside pictures or text boxes, and no tables for important information.
Never copy the whole ad or claim skills you do not have. Hidden or white text with key words can get you rejected, and false claims can cost you the job later.
Save the final CV as a PDF unless the ad asks for Word. Name the file clearly, like "Amina-Okafor-CV-Customer-Service.pdf", and keep it to two pages or less.
Step by step:
- Underline the key words in the ad: titles, skills, tools, languages, certificates.
- Mark the ones that are true for you.
- Use those exact words in your profile, skills and experience.
- Use simple headings and a plain layout; no text in pictures.
- Save as a PDF (or Word if asked) with your name and the job in the file name.
Words to know:
- Key words: the important words in a job ad: skills, tools, titles and certificates.
- ATS: applicant tracking system: software that collects CVs and searches them for key words.
- PDF: a file type that looks the same on every computer and phone.
Try it now: Find one real job ad. Underline ten key words. Tick the ones that are true for you and add at least five of them to your CV in the right places. Save it as a PDF with your name and the job in the file name.
You can now tailor your CV to a job ad with its key words and save it in a format employers and their software can read.

check.q: The ad asks for "bilingual French-English" and you speak both well. What do you do?
options: Write those words in your profile or languages section
Write it in white text so only the software sees it
Say you also speak five more languages
check.why: Using the ad's true key words where a person and the software can see them is honest tailoring.

check.q: Which layout is easiest for an applicant tracking system to read?
options: Text in many small text boxes
A table with all your skills in tiny cells
check.why: Software reads plain text under simple headings most reliably.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Before you send: spotting fake jobs and illegal recruiters
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a job offer and a recruiter for scam warning signs before you send your CV.
This lesson builds toward: Before you send your CV to a job or recruiter, you will check the offer for the warning signs of a fake job or an illegal recruiter, paying no fee and handing over no passport or original documents.
People looking for work, especially abroad, are a favorite target of scammers. The biggest warning sign: someone asks you to pay to get the job, for "processing", training, a medical, a visa or a placement. Honest employers do not charge you to get a job, and the International Labour Organization (ILO) fair recruitment principles say workers should not pay recruitment fees or related costs.
Other warning signs: an offer with no interview; very high pay for easy work; messages only on WhatsApp or a free email address; pressure to decide today; a company you cannot find on its own website; a request for your passport, original certificates or bank details; or a check sent to you with a request to send part of the money back.
Check before you apply. Search the company's real website and contact it using details you find yourself. For jobs abroad, check that the recruitment agency is licensed by your government's labor or migrant-worker office (for example the Department of Migrant Workers in the Philippines or the National Employment Authority in Kenya), and look up the destination country's official visa and work-permit pages.
Keep your own passport and original documents; send only copies when a real employer asks after an offer. If you suspect a scam or trafficking, stop contact and report it to your national police, labor ministry or the embassy. The IOM and ILO support migrants and publish fair-recruitment guidance.
Step by step:
- Never pay a fee to get a job or a recruiter's place.
- Find the company's real website and contact it yourself.
- For jobs abroad, check the agency's license with your government's labor or migrant-worker office.
- Read visa and work-permit rules only on official government or embassy websites.
- Keep your passport and originals; send copies only after a real offer.
- Stop and report anything that feels wrong.
Words to know:
- Recruitment fee: money a worker is asked to pay to get a job or a placement; fair recruitment says the worker should not pay it.
- Licensed agency: a recruitment agency your government has approved and can check.
- Trafficking: moving or holding people by force, fraud or debt to exploit their work.
Official sources:
- International Labour Organization (ILO): Fair recruitment
- US Federal Trade Commission: Job scams
Try it now: Final task: take your tailored CV and the job ad. Fill in this checklist on paper: Is there any fee? Did I find the company's real website myself? Is the recruiter licensed (for jobs abroad)? Am I keeping my passport and originals? Is my CV free of ID, passport and bank numbers? Only if every answer is safe, send your CV.
You can now check a job and a recruiter for scam warning signs and send an honest, tailored CV safely.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Right format for the country Longer than two pages, or personal details that do not fit the country or ad, or an ID or passport number included. Two pages or less, language, photo and personal details follow the ad and country, no ID, passport or bank numbers. Can explain which source (ad, employer page, country practice) decided each choice. Header and profile Missing contact details, no country code, an unprofessional email, or no profile. Working contact details with country code and a 3-4 line profile aimed at this job. The profile includes one clear result and the job title from the ad. Experience as results Entries list duties only, or informal work is left out. At least three entries, each starting with an action verb and including a number or concrete detail. Informal or unpaid work is shown with strong results, and every number can be explained. Qualifications and languages explained Local certificates are shown only as codes; languages have no level. Each qualification has its full name, place, country and year; each language has a level. Notes which official evaluation the employer accepts, or gives a language test and year. Tailored to the ad The CV could be for any job, or uses text in pictures or hidden key words. At least five true key words from the ad, simple headings, saved as a clearly named PDF. Learner can point to where each key word appears and why it is true. Checked before sending Checklist not done, or the offer asks for a fee or passport and the learner still applied. Scam checklist completed: no fee, company found independently, passport and originals kept. For a job abroad, the agency's license was checked with the government office. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: A recruiter offers you a hotel job in another country and asks for a "processing fee" first. What is this?
options: A sign of a good company
A warning sign; honest employers do not charge you to get a job
check.why: Asking workers to pay to get a job is the biggest scam warning sign.

check.q: A new employer wants to keep your passport "for safety" before you travel. What do you do?
options: Keep your own passport and check the offer with official sources
Give it to them; it is normal
Post a photo of it online
check.why: Keeping your passport protects you; taking workers' passports is a sign of forced labor and trafficking.
